Your denture didn’t change. Your jaw did.

The plate in your mouth is the same size it was the day it was made. The gum and bone it sits on are not. They’ve been shrinking a little every year since your teeth came out, and nobody told you.

Here’s what’s actually going on under your bottom plate.

Your top plate has the whole roof of your mouth to hold on to. That’s suction. That’s why it stays.

Your bottom plate doesn’t have that. It’s a thin horseshoe sitting on a ridge of gum, with nothing holding it down.

title: The Solution Doctors Found Too Late
body:
A man in his 60s died after years of using far too much zinc-containing denture cream.

His case was reported in a medical journal in 2010.

The story is real. And the amount of cream involved is a key part of it.

Poison Control describes people using two or more tubes a week, for years. Depending on the product, one tube should have lasted several weeks.

That extreme use meant swallowing much more of the cream than normal.

Doctors saw high zinc and low copper in these patients. They also found nerve damage and too few red blood cells.

Too much zinc can stop the body from getting enough copper. A severe lack of copper can harm both blood cells and nerves.

body:
A man in his 60s died after years of using far too much zinc-containing denture cream.

His case was reported in a medical journal in 2010.

The story is real. And the amount of cream involved is a key part of it.

Poison Control describes people using two or more tubes a week, for years. Depending on the product, one tube should have lasted several weeks.

That extreme use meant swallowing much more of the cream than normal.

Doctors saw high zinc and low copper in these patients. They also found nerve damage and too few red blood cells.

Too much zinc can stop the body from getting enough copper. A severe lack of copper can harm both blood cells and nerves.

In the fatal case, the man's nerve damage kept getting worse. The link to his excessive cream use was found late in his illness.

Copper treatment helped his blood problems. His nerve damage did not recover.

title: Read This If You Wear Dentures 👆
body:
I've been stopped 4 times at dentist appointments this year.

Not because something was wrong.

Because people kept asking what happened to my mouth.

The first time was in January.

Routine cleaning. Same office I'd been going to for almost 8 years.

Same hygienist.
Same dentist.

Same speech I usually got:
"A little more inflammation." "Your gums are irritated again." "Maybe try a different gum brush."

Same story. Every visit.

I'm 67.
Retired school teacher.
Fixed income. Social security. Clipping coupons.

I lost my teeth younger than I should have.

Back then you didn't go to the dentist unless something was already falling apart.

Grown up poor. Coffee and cigarettes for breakfast. Soda and candy while young. No one taught us any better.

By 58, I had full dentures.

And by 60, I was spending half my life trying to make them work.

Polident. Efferdent. Baking soda. Dawn dish soap.

title: The hospital rule nobody tells denture wearers
body:
Hospitals have a rule for patients who can't clean their own mouths.

It's there because of pneumonia, and nobody told me about it until I was 70.

I had my hip replaced last fall. Four nights in the hospital.

The first night, a nurse's aide named Tammy came in around nine with a little tray.

She asked for my teeth. She took them to the sink and scrubbed them. Then she cleaned my gums with a little foam swab, all the way around.

Every night. Every shift, the gums got checked.

I finally asked her, "Is this because I'm old?"

She laughed. "It's because you're in a bed. We do it for everybody. It's a rule."

"Why?"

"Pneumonia," she said. "The bacteria in your mouth get into your lungs. When you're lying down a lot and not moving, it happens easier. Keeping the mouth clean is one of the best ways we have to stop it."

I want to tell you something nobody told me for thirty-one years of nursing.

If you wear dentures — even if your mouth feels fine, even if your dentist says everything looks good, even if you brush and soak every single night — you almost certainly have gum disease right now.

You probably don't know you have it.

You almost certainly were not told by anyone whose job it was to tell you.

And it is doing something to the inside of your body that you have been blaming on aging for years.

I am writing this because I figured out what was happening to my own body six months ago, and once I knew what to look for, I started seeing it everywhere.

In my sister-in-law. In two of my closest friends. In the woman who cuts my hair. In every single denture-wearing patient I had cared for in the cardiac unit for the last decade and a half of my career.

Every one of them had it. None of them knew.

I only found out the truth after my stroke, and I wish I'd known it ten years sooner.

It's there because of pneumonia, and nobody told me about it until I was 70.

title: Read This If You Wear Dentures 👆
body:
I've been stopped 4 times at dentist appointments this year.

Not because something was wrong.

Because people kept asking what happened to my mouth.

The first time was in January.

Routine cleaning. Same office I'd been going to for almost 8 years.

Same hygienist.
Same dentist.

Same speech I usually got:
"A little more inflammation." "Your gums are irritated again." "Maybe try a different gum brush."

Same story. Every visit.

I'm 67.
Retired school teacher.
Fixed income. Social security. Clipping coupons.

I lost my teeth younger than I should have.

Back then you didn't go to the dentist unless something was already falling apart.

Grown up poor. Coffee and cigarettes for breakfast. Soda and candy while young. No one taught us any better.

By 58, I had full dentures.

And by 60, I was spending half my life trying to make them work.

Polident. Efferdent. Baking soda. Dawn dish soap.

title: The night I finally understood why my denture just wouldn’t stay put when I was eating.
body:
Have you ever caught yourself secretly avoiding your favorite foods because you don’t trust your denture to survive the very first bite?

I have. For years.

I told myself I was just being “careful,” that at my age you simply have to make a few compromises.
But the truth was much more uncomfortable.
I had stopped eating the things I loved. I treated my plate like a bomb technician treats a device that might explode.

Only soft foods. Tiny bites. Chew on the left, never the right. Don’t laugh while chewing. And always keep a napkin nearby—“just in case.”

The moment I finally reached my limit didn’t happen in a fancy restaurant.
It happened on an ordinary Sunday lunch at my daughter’s house.

Nothing special: roast, potatoes, vegetables, the usual chatter of grandchildren around the table.

My seven-year-old grandson Jamie held out the bowl and asked, “Grandma, do you want another piece?”
